planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, acidic soil in open to deep shade; this selection was made at the JC Raulston Arboretum and is considered one of the more cold-tolerant forms of the species.

directions: Chirimen is a distinctive selection of Japanese ardisia grown for its heavily quilted, deeply textured leaves with jagged, almost spiny-toothed margins, giving the low groundcover a coarser, more sculptural look than the smooth-leaved species. Like other Japanese ardisia forms it spreads gradually by underground rhizomes into a dense mat beneath trees and shrubs, tolerating deep shade and root competition where few other evergreen groundcovers persist. White summer flowers give way to round red berries that often hold on the plant into the following spring, adding winter interest to shaded beds. Its cold tolerance is reported to exceed that of plain-leaved Japanese ardisia, making it a reasonable choice for the cooler edge of its range in protected sites.

common_name: Hakuokan Japanese Ardisia (White King Variegated Marlberry)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container specimens in spring into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in part to full shade, sited out of drying wind and harsh afternoon sun that can scorch the white-margined leaves.

directions: Hakuokan, sold in the US trade under the name White King, is a collector-grade variegated form of Japanese ardisia prized for its broad, creamy-white leaf margins framing a gray-green center, with new growth often flushed pink before settling into its mature pattern. It forms a slow, refined groundcover creeping by rhizomes beneath shaded trees and along woodland path edges, brightening dark corners where solid-green groundcovers disappear into the gloom. Pale pink starry flowers appear in summer and are followed by small red berries that persist into winter. Because variegated forms are less vigorous and slightly less cold-hardy than the plain green species, give it consistent moisture, dappled rather than deep shade, and winter protection at the northern edge of its range.

common_name: Ito Fukurin Japanese Ardisia (Thread-Edge Variegated Marlberry)

planting.note: Establish divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, acidic soil in filtered to full shade; avoid direct midday sun, which fades and can scorch the thin variegated margins.

directions: Ito Fukurin is a finely variegated Japanese ardisia selection with a slender, thread-like white line tracing each leaf margin against gray-green foliage, a subtler effect than the broad-margined Hakuokan and one long favored by Japanese collectors of dwarf shade plants. Like other forms of the species it spreads slowly by underground rhizomes into a tidy, low, weed-suppressing carpet in shaded beds and woodland gardens, producing small pink-tinged flowers in summer followed by bright red berries. The narrow variegation is more delicate than heavily patterned forms and shows best in bright open shade rather than deep gloom or hot direct sun. Give it steady moisture and acidic, organically rich soil, and mulch over winter in the cooler parts of its range since variegated selections are somewhat less cold-hardy than the green species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in partial to deep shade in well-drained soil; site away from natural areas since, like the species, seed-grown plants can escape into hammocks and forest understory in the Gulf South.

directions: Pink Pearl is a fruit-color selection of coral ardisia that trades the species' typical coral-red berries for clusters of soft, pearly pink fruit held beneath the same dark, glossy, wavy-margined evergreen leaves, giving winter displays a softer color note than the standard red-berried form. It shares the species' remarkable tolerance for dry, root-filled shade beneath established trees, where few other flowering shrubs perform, and produces small white summer flowers ahead of the developing berry clusters. Because coral ardisia is classified as invasive in Florida and other Gulf Coast states, grow it only where berries can be removed before they ripen and drop, or choose a contained landscape setting away from natural woodlands. Otherwise culture matches the species: even moisture while establishing, then reasonable drought tolerance once rooted in.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; give this vigorous, large-growing selection extra room compared to the straight species since it develops into a small tree-sized screen over time.

directions: Bigfoot is a patented, fast-growing, large-statured Ternstroemia selection bred for bigger leaves and a more upright habit than the standard species, developing over time into a tall, dense evergreen screen or specimen tree in the humid Gulf South. New growth emerges light bronze-green, matures to glossy dark green, and picks up red-bronze tones again in cool weather, giving three seasons of foliage color on a plant that otherwise needs little care. It tolerates a wide range of soils from moist to fairly dry and sandy to heavy clay, though it performs best with consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained conditions, and it shrugs off the heat and humidity that stress boxwood and photinia. Because it grows considerably larger and faster than the species type, reserve it for screening, tall hedges, or specimen use rather than small foundation beds, and prune lightly after flowering if a more compact form is wanted.
